Is Black Pepper good or bad for your gut after 60? Scientists have tested what pepper does inside the stomach, but not in people over 60. In this video, we go through what the research does show, including a medicine warning that most people have never heard.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why the burn in your mouth tells you very little about what pepper does in your stomach
What happened when researchers placed black pepper directly into people’s stomachs, and why a second study with real meals found almost no damage
Why a stomach after 60 works differently, including lower stomach acid, slower digestion, and common medicines that irritate the stomach
How piperine, the main ingredient in black pepper, can affect how much of a medicine your body absorbs
Which medicines were involved in the studies, and the three questions to ask your pharmacist
What “black pepper extract,” “piperine,” and BioPerine on a supplement label really mean
What a small study found about pepper and feeling full
Three pepper myths you can skip, including “detox” and “cures constipation”
A simple six-rule pepper plan, plus the warning signs that mean you should call your doctor or 911

Watch to the end for the full plan and the pharmacist checklist.

If you found this helpful, please subscribe to Dr Wade Coolis. It costs you nothing, and it helps us continue making videos like this for you. Tap the bell so you never miss one.

Tell us in the comments: What is your first name, how old are you, and where are you watching from? And do you put pepper on almost everything, or only once in a while?

📚 Research and Sources

Myers BM, Smith JL, Graham DY. Effect of red pepper and black pepper on the stomach. American Journal of Gastroenterology, 1987.
Graham DY, Smith JL, Opekun AR. Spicy food and the stomach: evaluation by videoendoscopy. JAMA, 1988.
Zanzer YC, et al. Black pepper-based beverage induced appetite-suppressing effects without altering postprandial glycaemia, gut and thyroid hormones or gastrointestinal well-being. Food & Function, 2018.
Bano G, et al. Effect of piperine on bioavailability and pharmacokinetics of propranolol and theophylline in healthy volunteers. European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, 1991.
Bhardwaj RK, et al. Piperine, a major constituent of black pepper, inhibits human P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4. Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics, 2002.
Piperine drug interactions. Pharmacy Times, July 2017.
Shoba G, et al. Influence of piperine on the pharmacokinetics of curcumin in animals and human volunteers. Planta Medica, 1998.
Baik HW, Russell RM. Vitamin B12 deficiency in the elderly. Annual Review of Nutrition, 1999.

Disclaimer: This video is for general education only. It is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. The studies discussed were mostly done in young or middle-aged adults, and results may differ for you. If you take prescription medicines, have a stomach condition, or are thinking about starting a supplement, talk to your doctor or pharmacist first. Call 911 for chest pain or pressure.

#BlackPepper #SeniorHealth #GutHealth #MedicationSafety #HealthyAging

surprises. Blood sugar didn't change.

study. So, I wouldn't call pepper a
weight loss trick.

enjoyed don't taste quite as flavorful
as they used to.
A little black pepper, garlic, or other
herbs can make a meal more enjoyable
without adding extra salt.
If your doctor has asked you to watch
your sodium for your blood pressure,
that's a real help. That's not a
research finding. It's a simple everyday
idea that many dieticians suggest. And
it's a good reason to keep that grinder
on the table.
Fact number six. Three pepper myths you
can skip.
Now, let me clear up three claims you
may have seen online.
Myth number one. Black pepper cleans or
detoxes your gut. There's no good human
evidence for this. Your liver and
kidneys do the cleaning work, and pepper
isn't a cleanse.
Myth number two. Black pepper cures
constipation.
Some animal studies suggest piperine can
speed up the gut, but there's no solid
proof that a sprinkle of pepper fixes
constipation in people.
Fiber, water, and gentle movement have
much better support. And if the problem
keeps coming back, talk to your doctor.
Myth number three. Black pepper repairs
your gut bacteria.
This claim comes from early lab work.
The human proof isn't there yet. I'm not
saying pepper is useless. I'm saying
that if a video or a website promises
that a spice will fix your gut, be
careful. Look for studies in people, and
look at how much was used.
Fact number seven, your simple pepper
plan.
Now, let's put it all together into
something you can use. Here are six
simple rules.
Rule one, use pepper with food, not
alone. Skip the trend of swallowing
pepper in a glass of water, or taking it
on an empty stomach. The research that
showed irritation used pepper placed
alone into an empty stomach. Rule two,
watch your own pattern. If you often
have heartburn or an upset stomach, keep
a notebook for 2 weeks. Write down your
meals and your symptoms. If the heavy
pepper days match the bad days, cut back
for two or three weeks and see what
changes. Rule three, if you have reflux,
gastritis, or an ulcer, or you take
aspirin or arthritis pills, be extra
careful with heavy pepper, and ask your
doctor what's right for you. Also, try
smaller meals and avoid lying down for 2
to 3 hours after you eat. Rule four,
tell your pharmacist about your pepper
habit and your supplements. Bring the
three questions I gave you, and bring a
full list of everything you take,
including vitamins and herbal products.
Rule five, read supplement labels. If
you see piperine, black pepper extract,
or Bioperine, check with your pharmacist
before you start, especially if you take
any prescription medicine. Rule six,
know the warning signs. Call your doctor
soon if you have black or tar-like
stools, vomiting that looks like coffee
grounds, severe stomach pain, trouble
swallowing, or weight loss you can't
explain. And call 911 for chest pain or
pressure, because that can be your
heart, not your stomach. Now, notice
what's not on this list. There's no rule
that says to throw away your pepper
grinder. For most people, pepper on food
in everyday amounts is fine. The key is
to know your own body, and to know your
own medicines. Let's bring it together.
Black pepper is neither a gut villain
nor a gut cure. In young, healthy
people, it makes the stomach produce
more acid. And in the most extreme test,
it caused tiny signs of irritation. In
real meals, it showed almost no damage.
In one small study, it made people feel
fuller. And in a strong concentrated
form, piperine can change how the body
handles certain medicines. The big
lesson is that almost none of this was
tested in people your age. So, three
things matter most: how much you use,
what form it comes in, and how your own
body and your own medicines respond.
Keep those three straight and the
confusion clears up a lot. Before you
go, please remember this. This video is
for general education only. It is not
medical advice. If you take prescription
medicines, have a stomach condition, or
you're thinking about starting a
supplement, please talk to your doctor
or pharmacist first. Your own situation
always matters more than any general
guideline. Now, I'd like to ask you for
one small favor. I put out a video like
this every week. I check the research, I
explain it in plain words, and I leave
the warnings in because I believe you
deserve the truth. If you got even one
useful idea today, please subscribe. It
costs you nothing and it helps me
continue making videos like this for
you. Tap subscribe, tap the little bell,
and give this video a like so it can
reach other people who need it. And if
someone you love takes several
medicines, send this video to them. It
could save them a worry. And here's
what's coming next. Black pepper is only
one kitchen spice. In our next video,
we'll look at other everyday spices and
herbs, including turmeric, cinnamon, and
ginger. And which ones deserve a quick
word with your pharmacist. Make sure
you're subscribed so you don't miss it.
Now, tell me in the comments. Do you use
pepper on almost everything or only once
in a while? And did anything in this
video surprise you? Your kitchen is not
your enemy, and your body is smarter
than a headline. Take care of yourself
and I'll see you in the next video.

I will show you five ordinary morning

simple 5-minute routine that protects
it. Stay with me until the end, because
habit number five can save a life. I'm
Dr. Wade Collins. On this channel, my
one goal is to help seniors understand

Before we begin, tell me in the comments

I would love to hear from you. First,
you need to understand why the morning
is special.
When you wake up, your body does not
ease into the day. It switches on.
Stress hormones like cortisol rise and
peak about 30 to 45 minutes after you
wake. Your blood pressure climbs, your
heart rate goes up. At the same time,
your blood is at its thickest. You have
gone 7 or 8 hours without water, and
your platelets, the cells that help
blood clot, are more active. Studies
show that heart attacks and strokes
happen more often between early morning
and noon than at any other time of day.
This is not a flaw. It is how the human

What really happens to your body after 80? Researchers have found that aging comes in waves, with big shifts around 60 and 78. In this video, we go through five changes that tend to show up after 80, and what you can do about each one, starting this week. We also tell you which findings are proven and which are still being debated.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why balance gets weaker all at once, and why 1 in 4 older Americans falls every year (CDC)
A Tai Chi study of adults aged 70 to 92 that showed 55% fewer repeat falls
Why your muscles may respond more slowly to protein after 80, and how much protein experts suggest
How deep sleep changes with age, and what a 17-year Framingham Heart Study analysis found about sleep and dementia risk
Why your bones can lose inner structure, not just density, and what helps protect them
What “inflammaging” is, and the everyday habits linked to lower inflammation
A simple 7-day starter plan you can begin tomorrow

Watch to the end for the full first-week plan.

If you found this helpful, please subscribe to Dr Wade Coolis. It costs you nothing, and it helps us keep making videos like this for you. Tap the bell so you never miss one.

Tell us in the comments: What is your first name, how old are you, and where are you watching from? And which of the five changes surprised you the most?

📚 Research and Sources

Lehallier B, et al. Undulating changes in human plasma proteome profiles across the lifespan. Nature Medicine, 2019.
Bauer J, et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people (PROT-AGE Study Group). Journal of the American Medical Directors Association, 2013.
Himali JJ, et al. Association between slow-wave sleep loss and incident dementia. JAMA Neurology, 2023.

Which fruit is best for your eyes after 60? In this video, I compare 4 evening fruits for eye health, and show you the one with a real clinical study behind it.

In a small clinical trial, adults who ate a handful of one fruit for 90 days had a measurable rise in the protective pigment at the center of the retina. A lutein and zeaxanthin supplement did not show the same change. In this video, I explain what that study did and did not prove, and how to use the fruit safely.

IN THIS VIDEO
How your eye's built-in shield (macular pigment) works
Tart cherries: helpful for sleep, with little eye evidence
Kiwi: vitamin C and an easy evening habit
Papaya: a gentle source of vitamin A
Mulberries: promising lab research, not yet proven in people
Goji berries: the only fruit with a real human trial for macular pigment
How much to eat, and the three most common mistakes
Who should talk to a doctor first, including people who take blood thinners
3 eye myths, including carrots and supplements
Warning signs that need an eye doctor right away
3 questions to ask at your next eye appointment



Tell me in the comments where you are watching from and how old you are, and subscribe so you don't miss the next video. I read every comment and reply to each one.

IMPORTANT
No fruit cures or reverses eye disease. These effects build slowly, over weeks and months. If you take warfarin or another blood thinner, have diabetes, or have a food or sulfite allergy, talk to your doctor before adding goji berries or dried fruit. If you notice wavy lines, a dark spot in the center of your vision, or sudden vision changes, see an eye doctor right away. For sudden vision loss or stroke symptoms, call your local emergency number.

MEDICAL DISCLAIMER
This video is for education only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor or eye doctor about your health and your medicines.

SOURCES
Goji Berry Intake Increases Macular Pigment Optical Density in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Pilot Trial (Li et al., Nutrients, 2021)
AREDS2 Research Group, lutein and zeaxanthin with omega-3 for age-related macular degeneration (National Eye Institute)
Stimulatory effect of cyanidin 3-glycosides on the regeneration of rhodopsin (Matsumoto et al., Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2003)
Cyanidin-3-glucoside extracted from mulberry fruit can reduce N-methyl-N-nitrosourea-induced retinal degeneration in rats (Lee et al., 2013)

little each day, not winning the
lottery. If any video promises that one
fruit will restore your eyesight in a
week, please close it. Real health is
slower, and it is far more reliable.
Fruit is only one piece. Here is how to
build a simple eye-friendly evening.
Pair your fruit with a little fat. Plain
yogurt, a few walnuts or almonds, or a
spoon of nut butter. Remember, lutein
and zeaxanthin need fat to be absorbed
well.
Add leafy greens at dinner. Spinach,
kale, and collard greens are some of the
best food sources of lutein, and they
come with a lot more than eye support. A
cooked portion with a little olive oil
is easy to eat and easy to absorb. If
you take warfarin, keep your leafy
greens steady from day to day, and ask
your doctor, because the vitamin K in
greens affects that medicine.
Eggs are another good friend. Many
studies suggest the lutein and
zeaxanthin in egg yolks are absorbed
well because the yolk carries its own
fat. If your doctor limits eggs for you,
follow that advice.
Be kind to your eyes in the evening.
Read with good light. And if your eyes
feel dry or tired, take a break every 20
minutes and look at something far away
for 20 seconds.
And protect your sleep. Go to bed at a
regular time, keep your room dark and
cool, and limit caffeine late in the
day. Sleep is when your whole body
recovers.
Now, three quick myths. Keep count of
how many you believed. The third one
surprises almost everyone.
Myth one, carrots will fix my eyesight.
Carrots contain beta carotene, which
your body turns into vitamin A, and you
do need vitamin A. But if you already
get enough, extra carrots will not
sharpen your vision. The old story that
carrots help you see in the dark is
mostly a legend.
Myth two, my eye exam was fine, so I
don't need to think about this.
Many eye diseases are silent in the
early years. You can feel perfectly fine
while changes begin. That is why regular
exams matter, even when you see well.
Myth three, supplements are always
stronger than food. Not always. In the
goji study, the whole food raised
macular pigment and the supplement did
not. But supplements still have a role.
A large study from the National Eye
Institute called AREDS2
tested a specific vitamin and mineral
formula, and it helped slow progression
in some people who already had
intermediate AMD.
That is not the same as a general
multivitamin, and it is not for
everyone. Your eye doctor can tell you
whether it applies to you.
How many did you believe? If it was one
or two, you are in good company. Most
people do.
Let me make this simple. Two steps, not
10
Step one, make goji your anchor. A small
handful with yogurt or a few nuts five
evenings a week.
Step two, on the other evenings, rotate
one of the other fruits. Tart cherries,
kiwi, papaya, or a few mulberries if you
enjoy them.
Variety gives your eyes a wider range of
nutrients, and it keeps the habit from
becoming boring.
Before you start, take 2 minutes to
write down two numbers. On a scale of 1
to 10, how easy is it to read in normal
room light? And how tired do your eyes
feel at the end of the evening?
Check again in 30 days, and again at 90
days. This is not a medical test. It is
your own notebook, but it keeps you
honest and motivated, and you can show
it to your eye doctor.
And remember the basics, because they
matter even more than any fruit. Do not
smoke. Wear sunglasses with UV
protection. Keep your blood pressure and
blood sugar under control. And keep your
regular eye exams.
After 65, many people need a dilated eye
exam every 1 to 2 years. So, ask your
own eye doctor what schedule fits you.
Now, an important safety moment. Please
know these warning signs.
See your eye doctor soon if straight
lines look wavy or bent, or if you
notice a blurry or dark spot in the
center of your vision.
These can be early signs of macular
problems, and early treatment matters.
Get emergency help right away if you
have sudden vision loss in one eye, a
sudden shower of new floaters with
flashes of light, or a dark curtain or
shadow moving across your vision.
And if sudden vision changes come with a
drooping face, a weak arm, or trouble
speaking, call your emergency number
immediately. That can be a stroke.
Fruit is a helper. It is never a reason
to wait.
At your next eye appointment, ask three
questions. One, do you see any early
changes in my macula or retina that I
should know about? Two, do any of my
medicines affect which foods are safe
for me, especially blood thinners?
Three, would the AREDS2 supplement
formula be right for me? Write them down
if you need to. Any good eye doctor will
welcome these questions, and asking them
shows you are taking an active role in
your own care. Let's bring it together.
Your eyes have a built-in shield, and
that shield needs to be refilled from
food. Tart cherries, kiwi, and papaya
are tasty helpers. Mulberries are a
promising idea, but not yet a proven
one. And goji berries have the strongest
evidence of the four. A small study that
measured a real change in the macula.
None of this is a cure. All of it is a
small, kind habit repeated every
evening. And small habits are how most
people protect their independence. If
this video helped you, share it with one
person who worries about their eyesight.
A small handful of fruit and a few
minutes of information could mean a lot
to them. And please tell me in the
comments where you are watching from and
how old you are. And subscribe so you
don't miss the next video. I read every
comment and reply to each one. Which
fruit will you try first? In the next
video, I will show you three everyday
habits that quietly strain your eyes and
the simple fixes. You won't want to miss
it. Take care of yourself and take care
of your eyes. I'll see you in the next
video.

Stool stuck in the rectum and can't push it out? This video explains what's happening inside your body, why straining makes it worse, and what you can safely do, step by step. It also covers the warning signs that mean you should stop home care and get medical help.

This one is written for adults over 55 and for the people who care for them. It's an uncomfortable subject, and a lot of people deal with it quietly. You don't have to.

IN THIS VIDEO
Why this is not just constipation
What is actually happening inside your colon
Why a stuck stool is more serious than most people think
Why older adults are hit hardest
What to do now, step by step (and when to go to the ER)
Recovery: the first 48 hours
How to keep it from happening again

WHEN TO GET HELP RIGHT AWAY
Go to urgent care or the emergency room if you have severe or worsening belly pain, a swollen or hard belly, vomiting, fever, blood from the rectum, confusion or dizziness, chest pain or fainting, or you cannot urinate.

REFERENCES
1. Madsen JL, Graff J. Effects of ageing on gastrointestinal motor function. Age and Ageing. 2004;33(2):154-159.
2. Phillips PA, et al. Reduced thirst after water deprivation in healthy elderly men. New England Journal of Medicine. 1984;311(12):753-759.
3. Rey E, et al. A nation-wide study of prevalence and risk factors for fecal impaction in nursing homes. PLoS ONE. 2014;9(8):e105281.
4. Fecal Impaction. StatPearls (updated July 2023).
5. Malone JC, Thavamani A. Physiology, Gastrocolic Reflex. StatPearls (updated May 2023).
6. Modi RM, et al. Implementation of a defecation posture modification device: impact on bowel movement patterns in healthy subjects. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology. 2019.
7. U.S. FDA safety alerts on sodium phosphate laxatives and enemas (2006, 2014).
8. Imodium (loperamide) prescribing label, U.S. FDA.

IMPORTANT
This video is for general education only. It is not medical advice and it does not replace a visit with your own doctor. If you have heart disease, kidney disease, or take blood thinners, ask your doctor or pharmacist before using any suppository or enema. Do not stop any prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor first.

If this helped you, please share it with someone who might be struggling in silence, and subscribe for more plain-language health talks for adults over 55.

subtitles.plaintext:
Picture this. It's Sunday afternoon.
You've been in the bathroom for 25
minutes. Your legs are going numb. Your
face is flushed. You can feel it, low
and heavy, sitting right there, and it
will not move.
You get up. You tell yourself it will
sort itself out.
Then that evening, something strange
happens. A little liquid leaks out. You
think, "Good. Maybe it's finally
loosening."
It isn't.
Hear this clearly. This is not just
constipation. Constipation is a slow
day. This is your body sending you a
warning that something solid is lodged
where your body can no longer push it
out. And every hour you wait, it gets
harder.
My name is Dr. Wade Collins, and today
we are having a real, honest
conversation about stool that is stuck
in the rectum. Doctors call it fecal
impaction. It is common after 55. It is
rarely talked about, and far too many
people suffer through it alone,
embarrassed, afraid to say a word.
Today, I'll show you what is happening
inside your body, why it is more
dangerous than most people realize, who
it hits hardest, exactly what to do,
step-by-step, and how to make sure it
never happens again.
Some of this will feel uncomfortable.
That's fine. Knowledge gives you
dignity.
If any of this sounds like your last few
days, or someone you love, drop the word
yes in the comments right now. You are
not alone.
Let's begin. Let's start with the
plumbing. Your large intestine, the
colon, is about 5 ft long. It climbs the
right side of your belly, crosses under
your ribs, and comes down the left side.
The final stretch is the rectum. Think
of the rectum as a waiting room. Stool
arrives soft. It waits a moment. Your
brain says, "Now." And it leaves. Your
colon has two jobs: move waste forward,
and pull water out of that waste along
the way. Both matter. How does it move?
Imagine a crowd at a stadium doing the
wave. Nobody walks anywhere, yet the
wave travels all the way around the
stadium. Your colon does the same thing.
Muscle squeeze in sequence, wave after
wave, pushing everything forward.
Doctors call this peristalsis. That wave
depends on three things: healthy nerves,
movement, and water. Now watch what
happens when it fails. Day one, the wave
slows. Stool lingers in the lower colon,
but the colon doesn't know the wave has
slowed. It keeps absorbing water. Day
two, day three. Picture a wet sponge
left on the edge of the sink. On day
one, it's soft. By the end of the week,
it's a brick. Stool does exactly the
same thing: drier, denser, larger. Day
four, day five. That dry mass settles
into the rectum. The rectum stretches
just to hold it. And here's the cruel
part. A rectum stretched for too long
goes numb to the stretch. The signal
fades. So the urge to go gets weaker
while the problem gets bigger. The end
point looks like this. A firm, dry mass,
sometimes the size of a fist, packed in
like a cork in a bottle. The muscles
that should push it out simply cannot
get a grip. That is fecal impaction. Not
slow, stuck. And if you are a caregiver,
listen closely. Your loved one may never
say "I'm stuck." They may be
embarrassed, or they may not be able to
tell you. Watch for restlessness, a poor
appetite, a swollen belly, or sudden
leaking. Those can be the only clues. If
you're learning something new, tap the
like button. It helps this reach someone
who needs it. Most people hear
constipation and think, "A cup of prune
juice and I'll be fine by morning." Not
this time. When something is lodged like
a cork, swallowing more laxatives pushes
more stool up against the blockage. That
can mean cramping, pain, and a bigger
problem, not a smaller one. So, please
hold off on strong oral laxatives until
you have a plan.
Now, let's talk about what that mass
does to its neighbors.
Your pelvis is like a crowded hallway.
The rectum, the bladder, the nerves, and
in men, the prostate, all share very
tight space.
When the rectum is packed and stretched,
it leans on everything around it. The
most common result is urinary trouble.
You feel a constant need to go, but only
a trickle comes out. Sometimes, nothing.
I have seen people treated for a bladder
infection who simply had a packed rectum
pressing on the bladder from behind.
Treat the impaction, and the urinary
symptoms often ease.
The pressure can also irritate nerves,
causing an ache in the lower back or
down the legs.
Now, the cruelest trick of all,
overflow.
Above the blockage, your intestines keep
making liquid. That liquid has to go
somewhere, so it seeps around the edges
of the hard mass and leaks out. It looks
exactly like diarrhea. It is not, and
some people reach for anti-diarrhea
medicine. Please, don't. That medicine
slows your gut even more. You'd be
shutting down the only route your body
has left. If you have leaking liquid
stool along with days of not truly
emptying, talk to a doctor before taking
anything to stop it.
One more thing, especially for
caregivers.
In older adults, a packed bowel doesn't
always announce itself with pain.
Sometimes, it shows up as confusion, or
agitation, or a sudden loss of appetite.
Someone with memory problems may simply
become restless and irritable, and
nobody connects it to the bowel.
So, if a person you care for suddenly
seems off, ask about their bowel habits.
It is a simple question, and it can
change everything.
Finally, your heart.
When you strain hard, you hold your
breath and bear down. Doctors call this
the Valsalva maneuver. It makes pressure
in your chest surge, and your blood
pressure can spike sharply. For someone
with heart disease or very high blood
pressure, that is a real risk. Some
people even faint on the toilet from
straining. That is why cardiologists
tell their patients to avoid straining.
So, I'll say it again. Stop pushing. If
this is helping you, type the number two
in the comments so I know you're still
with me. Fecal impaction is not random.
It gathers in older adults, and
especially in people with limited
mobility.
Studies of nursing home residents show
that it is a common problem in that
setting. Far more common than most
families expect. There are four main
reasons.
One, the wave slows down.
Research in the journal Age and Ageing
found that colon transit is slower in
older adults compared with younger ones.
The nerves and muscles that drive
peristalsis simply weaken over time.
Two, thirst goes quiet.
A well-known study in the New England
Journal of Medicine found that after
going without water, healthy older men
felt much less thirsty than younger men,
even though their bodies needed fluid
more. So, you can be dehydrated and feel
nothing. And your colon, always hungry
for water, takes it from the stool.
Three, medications.
Many commonly prescribed drugs slow the
gut. Opioid pain medicines, iron pills,
some blood pressure medicines, allergy
pills, certain antidepressants, calcium
and antacid products.
If you take several of these, the effect
adds up. Please do not stop any
medication on your own, but do tell your
doctor or pharmacist if you've been
constipated. They can often adjust the
plan.
Four, lifelong habits.
Many of us grew up believing bathroom
needs should be private and quiet. So,
we held it in. At work, on the road, at
someone else's house.
Year after year, that teaches the rectum
to ignore the signal.
Add little daily movement and the whole
system slows down.
And there is a fifth quiet factor.
Sitting or lying down most of the day.
After a hospital stay, a fall, or
surgery, people move less. They eat
less. They drink less. And the gut slows
right along with the body.
If that sounds like your household right
now, pay extra attention to everything
we cover next.
Notice something. Most of these are
fixable. That's the good news. Now,
let's talk about what to do.
Rule number one, before any product and
before any position, stop straining.
I know your body is screaming at you to
push harder, but a dry, hardened mass
does not respond to pushing.
Pushing only spikes your blood pressure
and tires you out. Put the effort down.
Breathe. We're going to do this the calm
way.
A quick note first. This is general
education, not a personal prescription.
If you have heart disease, kidney
disease, or you're on blood thinners,
check with your doctor or pharmacist
before using any of these.
Step one, a glycerin suppository.
You can buy these without a
prescription.
Follow the label for the dose. Do not
use more than the package says.
Lie on your left side with your knees
bent. Warm water-based lubricant on the
tip helps.
Insert it gently, breathe slowly, and
stay lying down.
Now, wait. Many people need 20 to 30
minutes. Don't rush to the toilet at 10.
You'll only expel the suppository.
Step two, gentle movement.
If nothing has happened, get up slowly.
Walk around your home for 15 to 20
minutes. Have a warm drink. Movement
wakes up the gut. If walking is hard,
march in place while holding a counter,
or simply change position.
Then, if you're comfortable, you can
rest and try again after.
Step three, a gentle enema.
If steps one and two haven't worked, ask
your pharmacist about an enema. And here
is something important. Many
store-bought enemas contain sodium
phosphate. In older adults, especially
those with kidney problems or
dehydration, repeated use can be
dangerous.
A mineral oil enema is often a gentler
choice. Use it once, exactly as labeled.
Do not repeat it again and again.
Lie on your left side, insert slowly,
hold as long as is comfortable. And
please, do not try to dig or scoop with
your fingers at home. It can tear
delicate tissue, cause bleeding, and in
some people trigger a drop in heart rate
and blood pressure.
Step four, medical care.
And this is not defeat. Go to urgent
care or the emergency room if any of
these happen.
Severe or worsening belly pain.
A swollen, hard belly.
Vomiting.
Fever.
Blood from the rectum.
Confusion or dizziness.
Chest pain or fainting.
Or you cannot urinate.
Or simply, you've tried these steps and
nothing has worked. Don't be
embarrassed. Clinicians treat this every
single day.
They can check how large the blockage
is. They can use stronger treatments,
and when needed, gently break up and
remove the mass by hand, often with
comfort medication or sedation. It's
routine, it's safe, and most people feel
enormous relief afterward.
If you're still with me, type the number
four in the comments. Once things have
cleared, your body needs a gentle
landing.
The rectal tissue has been stretched and
irritated. For the first day or two, you
may feel sore, a little raw, or see a
streak of blood. Mild soreness is
common. Heavy bleeding or worsening pain
is not. Call your doctor.
For comfort, try a warm sitz bath. Sit
in a few inches of plain warm water for
10 to 15 minutes a couple of times a
day. No soaps or additives.
For food, think soft and gentle.
Oatmeal, ripe banana, cooked carrots,
soups and broths. Hold off on tough, dry
foods for a day or two. And drink on a
schedule, not when you feel thirsty.
Remember, your thirst signal may be
quiet. One more thing. Please don't rush
back to strong laxatives the moment you
feel better. Let your bowels settle.
And start a simple notebook. Write down
the date of each bowel movement and how
it felt. Soft, hard, easy, difficult.
That small record gives your doctor real
information, and it helps you notice
trouble early. Then, while this is
fresh, make two calls. First, your
primary care doctor to review your
medications for constipating side
effects. Second, if this has happened
before, a gastroenterologist to check
for any narrowing or underlying problem.
An impaction is a crisis.
But crises are what happen when the
daily system fails. So, let's build a
system.
One, water on a clock. Set four alarms.
Morning, noon, afternoon, evening. One
full glass each time. If you've been
told to limit fluids for your heart or
kidneys, ask your doctor what is right
for you.
Two, move every day. 20 to 30 minutes of
walking is one of the best things you
can do for your gut. Even gentle,
supported movement counts.
Three, fiber, slowly. Oats, lentils,
beans, cooked fruits. Add a little at a
time. Too much too quickly leads to gas
and bloating, and then people give up.
Four, train your reflex. After a meal,
your colon naturally becomes more
active. Doctors call this the
gastrocolic reflex. Use it. Sit on the
toilet after breakfast at the same time
each day, feet resting on a small stool,
knees above your hips. Give yourself 5
to 10 unhurried minutes. No pushing.
Over weeks, your body relearns the
rhythm. Here is a simple rule to
remember. If you go 3 days without a
bowel movement, don't wait. Increase
your water, take a walk, and call your
doctor or pharmacist for advice. Early
action is gentle action. Waiting for the
crisis is the hard way. And one warning,
be careful with stimulant laxatives.
They work fast, but using them daily can
leave your bowel dependent on them. Ask
your doctor about gentler options, such
as fiber, stool softeners, or osmotic
laxatives as part of a long-term plan.
If you've made it this far, thank you. I
know this isn't an easy topic, but
silence is what makes this problem
dangerous, and knowledge is what gives
you your dignity back.
If this video helped you, do one thing
for me. Send it to someone in your life
who may be suffering in silence. In
almost every family, that person exists.
This could be exactly what they needed
to hear.
And if you are the one caring for
someone else, thank you. What you do is
not small.
Asking the awkward question, noticing
the quiet change, and getting help early
can spare someone a lot of pain.
If you got value today, hit like and
subscribe for more honest conversations
about your health after 55.
Drink your water, keep moving, and be
kind to your body. It has carried you a
long way.
I'm Dr. Wade Collins. I'll see you in
the next one.

How often should you shower or bathe after 60? New research and skin experts suggest that for many older adults, fewer showers, done the right way, may be better for the skin, and safer too. In this video, we go through seven facts, and we tell you which ones are strong and which come with a warning.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why your skin after 60 is thinner and drier, and how a daily hot shower can make itching worse
The real science behind “older person smell” (2-nonenal), and why more showers may not fix it
Why hot water can make your blood pressure drop, and what Japan’s bath-safety rules can teach us
How your skin cleans and renews itself, and why washing smart beats scrubbing hard
What the CDC found about bathroom falls and injuries, and the simple changes that help prevent them
How dry, cracked skin can let germs in, and how to protect it
A simple five-minute daily wash for the areas that matter most, plus how often most healthy seniors can bathe
A bathroom safety checklist: grab bars, non-slip mats, a shower chair, and more

Watch to the end for the full daily routine and the safety checklist.

If you found this helpful, please subscribe to Dr Wade Coolis. It costs you nothing, and you’ll get a new video every week about staying strong, healthy, and independent. Tap the bell so you never miss one.

Haze S, et al. 2-Nonenal newly found in human body odor tends to increase with aging. Journal of Investigative Dermatology, 2001.

I want you to stop and think for a
second. When was the last day you did
not take a shower?
Maybe you can't even remember.
For most of us, a morning shower is as
normal as brushing our teeth.
We were taught that a daily shower means
you are clean, healthy, and polite.
But what if I told you that for many
people over 60, that daily habit may be
drying out your skin, making you itchy,
and in some cases, putting you at risk
of a faint or a fall?
I'm not saying this to scare you. I'm
saying it because the fact surprised me.
In just 1 year, more than 234,000
Americans were treated in emergency
rooms for injuries in the bathroom. That
comes from the CDC.
And the risk goes up as we get older.
At the same time, skin doctors are
saying that older skin often does better
with fewer showers, not more.
So today, I will answer a question
almost nobody asks their doctor.
How often should you really bathe after
60?
I'll give you seven facts. Some are
comforting, some come with a warning,
and I'll tell you which is which because
you deserve the truth, not hype. Here is
what's coming. We'll look at why your
skin plays by different rules now. We'll
talk about the real science behind what
people call older person smell, and why

Is your bedtime snack hurting your kidneys? Or helping them?

In this video, a doctor explains the best fruit to eat before bed for healthy kidneys, and which fruits to be careful with.

Your blood pressure is supposed to drop at night. That rest is good for your heart and your kidneys. But salty snacks can get in the way. The right swap can help.

This video is for adults over 60 and the people who love them. About 1 in 3 adults over 65 has kidney disease. Most don't know it.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
• Why your blood pressure should drop at night
• Why no fruit can cure kidney disease (and what fruit can do)
• Blueberries and other berries: what the research shows
• Apples: the easiest, cheapest choice
• The potassium warning most people never hear
• Cranberries and UTIs: who they may help
• Tart cherries and sleep: what one small study found
• What matters more than the fruit
• A simple 7-night plan to start tonight

4 QUESTIONS TO ASK YOUR DOCTOR
1. What is my kidney function (eGFR)?
2. Is there protein (albumin) in my urine?
3. What is my potassium level?
4. Given my medicines, are there foods I should limit?

CALL YOUR DOCTOR OR 911 IF YOU HAVE
Burning or urgency with fever. Pain in your back or side. Sudden confusion. A fluttering heartbeat with weakness. Fainting. Chest pain.


📚 RESEACH SOURCES:
1. CDC. Chronic Kidney Disease in the United States, 2023.
2. Johnson SA, et al. Daily blueberry consumption improves blood pressure and arterial stiffness in postmenopausal women with pre- and stage 1-hypertension. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 2015;115(3):369-377.
3. Williams G, et al. Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023;4:CD001321.
4. Pigeon WR, et al. Effects of a tart cherry juice beverage on the sleep of older adults with insomnia: a pilot study. Journal of Medicinal Food. 2010;13(3):579-583.
5. National Kidney Foundation. 40 Low Potassium Fruits and Vegetables to Add to Your Grocery List.
6. NIDDK / National Institutes of Health. Potassium: tips for people with chronic kidney disease.

DISCLAIMER
This video is for general education only. It is not medical advice, diagnosis or treatment, and it does not replace a visit with your own doctor, pharmacist or kidney dietitian. If you have kidney disease, diabetes, heart disease, or take prescription medicines, talk to your care team before changing your diet or using any supplement, salt substitute or juice. No food or fruit can cure kidney disease. The people described in this video (Ruth, Gene, Harold, Evelyn and Linda) are fictional examples, and individual results will differ. Never ignore or delay medical care because of something you saw in a video.

If this helped you, please share it with someone over 60, and subscribe. It costs you nothing.

What do your feet reveal about diabetes after 60? In this video, I count down 9 signs of diabetes in your feet, from cold feet and color changes to burning, tingling, and numbness, plus a 30-second foot check you can do at home.

I'm Dr. Wade Collins, and this channel helps seniors understand their health in simple words.

Diabetes signs in feet can appear before a blood test catches the problem, because high blood sugar can damage the nerves and small blood vessels in the feet first. In this video, I explain what each sign may mean, what else can cause it, and what to do next. If you have noticed diabetic neuropathy symptoms, cold feet, swollen feet, or sores that heal slowly, this video is for you.

IN THIS VIDEO
Why the feet show trouble first, and the CDC numbers for adults over 65
Sign 9: Dry, flaky, cracked heels that ignore lotion
Sign 8: Hair loss on toes and shins, and shiny skin
Sign 7: Thick, yellow toenails and fungus between the toes
Sign 6: Cold feet and feet color change (pale, blue, or red)
Sign 5: Calf cramps when you walk (claudication)
Sign 4: Burning feet at night, tingling feet, and pins and needles (peripheral neuropathy)
Sign 3: Calluses, blisters, and sores that heal slowly
How to check your feet for diabetes at home: a 30-second test
Sign 2: A change in foot shape, or a swollen, warm foot
Sign 1: Loss of protective sensation, and the monofilament test
How to read the pattern, and which tests to ask for (A1C and fasting blood sugar)
Red flags that need same-day care
A 2-minute daily diabetic foot care routine



Tell me in the comments where you are watching from and how old you are, and subscribe so you don't miss the next video. I read every comment and reply to each one.

IMPORTANT
None of these signs proves you have diabetes. Many have other causes, so the pattern matters more than any single sign. Ask your doctor about an A1C test, a fasting blood sugar test, and a foot exam with a monofilament test. Get same-day care for an open sore with spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or fever. Call your local emergency number for a sudden cold, pale, or blue foot with severe pain.

MEDICAL DISCLAIMER
This video is for education only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor about your health and your medicines.

SOURCES AND RESOURCES
CDC, National Diabetes Statistics Report (diabetes and prediabetes in adults 65 and older, and undiagnosed diabetes)
CDC, Diabetes in the United States (diabetes as the leading cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputations)
American Diabetes Association, Standards of Care in Diabetes: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care
American Diabetes Association Foot Care Interest Group, Comprehensive Foot Examination and Risk Assessment (Diabetes Care, 2008)
Diabetes UK, Your Annual Foot Check (what a foot check should include, and signs of nerve and blood supply damage)
Mount Sinai Health Library, Diabetes: Taking Care of Your Feet (monofilament test, dry skin, and foot care tips)

What happens when you eat peanut butter every day after 60? New research suggests a simple daily spoonful of natural peanut butter may help with strength, heart health, blood sugar, sleep, and more. In this video, we go through the science one part of the body at a time, and we tell you which findings are strong and which come with a warning.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why many adults over 60 don’t get enough magnesium, and how everyday foods can help fill the gap
What a recent six-month study from Deakin University found about peanut butter and leg strength in older adults
How niacin (vitamin B3) has been linked to slower memory decline, and why this kind of study can’t prove cause and effect
How peanut butter affects blood sugar, and what a large Harvard study of more than 83,000 women found
What big studies say about peanuts and heart health
Whether peanut butter can really help you sleep (the honest answer might surprise you)
How magnesium and phosphorus fit into bone health
How to pick the right jar: what to look for on the label, what to avoid, and the grocery store mistake that cancels out many of the benefits
How much to eat, when to eat it, and the best foods to pair it with
Who should check with a doctor first

Small daily food choices add up as we get older. Watch to the end for the full label guide.

If you found this helpful, please subscribe to Dr Wade Coolis. It costs you nothing, and you’ll get a new video every week about staying strong, healthy, and independent. Tap the bell so you never miss one. And tell us in the comments: what is your first name, where are you watching from, and how old are you?

📚 Research and Sources

Deakin University, Institute for Physical Activity and Nutrition. Peanut butter and muscle power in older adults, 6-month randomised controlled trial. Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, 2026.
Ryder KM, et al. Magnesium intake from food and supplements and bone mineral density in healthy older adults. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, 2005.
Morris MC, et al. Dietary niacin and the risk of incident Alzheimer’s disease and of cognitive decline. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry, 2004.

NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Magnesium fact sheet for health professionals.
U.S. Food and Drug Administration: phase-out of partially hydrogenated oils.
American Heart Association: replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat.
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force: osteoporosis screening recommendation.

Disclaimer: This video is for general education only. It is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. The studies discussed show links, not guarantees, and results vary from person to person. Talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian before changing your diet, especially if you have a health condition, take medicine, or have a food allergy.

for a jar that says no salt added, and
compare the numbers on the labels.
If this video is helping you, I have a
question.
Tell me in the comments which one
matters most to you right now? Your
muscles, your brain, your blood sugar,
or your heart? I really want to know
what is on your mind. It helps me decide
what to make next. Now, let's talk about
sleep. It may be the most forgotten part
of healthy aging. I don't mean just
falling asleep. Most of us can do that.
I mean deep, restful sleep. The kind
where you wake up feeling like your body
truly rested. That is when your brain
sorts out your memories, your muscles
repair themselves, and your body fights
off illness.
It is also tied to your heart, your
blood pressure, and your mood.
After 60, deep sleep gets harder to
keep. Many of us wake up more often at
night. We spend less time in the deepest
kind of sleep. And our body makes less
melatonin, the natural sleep hormone, as
we age.
You may have heard that peanut butter
helps you sleep because it has
tryptophan. It's true that it has
tryptophan. That's the same thing people
blame for feeling sleepy after a big
turkey dinner. Your body uses it to make
melatonin. But I owe you the real story,
not a sales pitch.
In 2022, scientists put together the
results of many studies on tryptophan
and sleep. They found that tryptophan
pills, especially at 1 g or more, cut
down the time people spent awake during
the night. That sounds good. But here is
the catch. A serving of peanut butter
has only about a tenth of a gram of
tryptophan. That is far less than the
pills used in those studies.
So, peanut butter by itself is not a
sleep aid. If someone tells you it is,
they are overselling it. So, why bring
it up at all? Because a small evening
snack can still help a little.
For some people, going to bed a bit
hungry is exactly what wakes them up at
3:00 in the morning. A small snack with
a little protein and a little whole
grain, like a teaspoon or two of peanut
butter on a whole grain cracker or
stirred into a small bowl of warm
oatmeal, can calm your stomach. It has
no caffeine and no sugar rush. Just keep
it small and try to finish eating an
hour or two before you lie down.
A big snack right before bed can cause
heartburn and make your sleep worse.
The bigger helpers for sleep are simple
ones.
Get outside in the morning light. Go to
bed and wake up at the same time every
day, even on weekends.
Stop drinking coffee and tea after
lunch.
Keep your bedroom cool and dark.
Move your body during the day.
And if you snore loudly, wake up
gasping, or feel worn out even after a
full night in bed, please see your
doctor.
Sleep apnea is common in older people
and it can be treated. So, here is
something to think about. Are you
sleeping deeply or are you just
sleeping? There is a big difference and
it matters a little more with every
birthday. Ask most people how to protect
their bones and you'll hear one word,
calcium. Maybe vitamin D, too. Both
matter. But bones are built by a team
and two helpers hardly ever get
mentioned. They are phosphorus and
magnesium.
Here is how it works. Your bones are
made of a hard mineral frame. Calcium
and phosphorus lock together to build
it. Calcium gets all the attention, but
without enough phosphorus, that frame
can't form well. Magnesium helps your
body turn vitamin D into the kind it can
actually use. So, if you take vitamin D
and calcium, but you are low on
magnesium, you may not be getting all
the good from what you are paying for.
Two spoonfuls of natural peanut butter
give you roughly 8 to 10% of the
phosphorus you need in a day and about
12% of your magnesium. That comes from
food, not a pill. And food is how your
body likes to get its nutrients because
you also get protein, fiber, and other
good things in the same bite.
What does the research say?
A study in the Journal of the American
Geriatrics Society looked at just over
2,000 people between 70 and 79 years
old. Scientists measured how strong
their bones were and they checked how
much magnesium these people got from
food and pills. Among the white people
in the study, those who got more
magnesium had stronger bones, even after
the scientists took into account
calcium, vitamin D, body weight,
smoking, and exercise. And remember that
number from earlier? Only about one in
four people in the study got enough
magnesium. Now, here is the warning.
This study took one snapshot in time. It
did not follow people for years, and the
link was not seen in the black people in
the study. So, it shows a link. It does
not prove that eating more peanut butter
will protect your hips. Please don't
think of peanut butter as a bone
medicine. It is not one. Here is what I
would say instead. The basics of bone
health have not changed. Get enough
calcium and vitamin D. Get enough
protein because your bones need it, too.
Do exercise that makes your bones work,
like walking, and some strength
exercise. Don't smoke. Make your home
safe so you don't fall, and ask your
doctor about a bone density test, which
is usually advised for women 65 and
older. Inside that bigger picture,
getting enough magnesium and phosphorus
from everyday food is a smart detail,
and a spoonful of peanut butter can help
with that. Why does this matter so much?
Because a broken hip is one of the most
serious injuries an older person can
have, and many people never get back the
independence they had before.
Most of us do nothing for our bones
until something breaks. Small habits
everyday, started early, are how we make
the odds better. All right, you stayed
with me this long, so let's make sure
you walk away with something you can
use. Because all of this can go to waste
if you buy the wrong jar, eat it the
wrong way, or pile it on top of
everything else you already eat.
Rule number one is to read the label
before you put a jar in your cart.
This is the grocery store mistake I told
you about at the start. Turn the jar
around and look at the list of
ingredients. The best peanut butter has
one or two things on it. Peanuts and
maybe a little salt. That is all. If you
see added sugar in any form like sugar,
honey, molasses, or corn syrup, think
twice because that works against the
blood sugar help we talked about. If you
see palm oil or hydrogenated oil, it is
there to keep the jar from separating
and it adds bad fat. One kind called
partially hydrogenated oil was the main
source of artificial trans fat. It is
mostly been taken out of our food in the
United States, but it is still smart to
check.
And here is the trap that catches so
many people. Be careful with jars that
say reduced fat. It sounds healthier,
but when the fat comes out, companies
often put extra sugar and fillers in.
The calories barely go down and you lose
the very fat that makes peanut butter so
useful. Pick the regular natural jar
instead.
Natural peanut butter will separate.
You'll see oil on top. That is not a
flaw. It is a sign that nothing
artificial was added to hold it
together. Stir it well when you open it.
Keeping the jar upside down for a while
before you open it can make stirring
easier and keeping it in the fridge
after you stir it slows the separating.
Rule number two is to know your serving
size and to swap not add. Two spoonfuls
of natural peanut butter is about 190
calories, about 16 g of fat, about 7 g
of protein, and about 2 g of fiber. The
studies we talked about used amounts
around that size. If you are watching
your weight, one spoonful is still worth
it. And remember what the scientists
kept saying. Peanut butter works best
when it takes the place of something
less healthy like jam on white bread, a
pastry, or a bag of chips. It does not
work as a bonus on top of what you
already eat. Half a jar in one sitting
is just a lot of calories.
Rule number three is to pick a time you
will stick with.
The truth is that the research does not
point to one magic hour. Many people
like it at breakfast on whole grain
toast or in oatmeal because it keeps
them full for hours.
Others like it as an afternoon snack
that beats the 2:00 slump.
After a walk or a strength workout is
also a good time because your muscles
can use the protein.
Many experts on aging also say it helps
to spread your protein over the whole
day and not eat most of it at dinner.
So, the best time is the one you will
actually do.
Rule number four is to pair it the smart
way.
Peanut butter on white bread with a
glass of juice is still a lot of fast
sugar. Peanut butter on whole grain
toast with banana slices or on apple
slices or stirred into plain Greek
yogurt or oatmeal is a very different
story. You get more fiber, you get more
protein, and you stay full longer.
Celery sticks and whole grain crackers
work well, too. And so does a small
spoonful on top of a bowl of berries.
Rule number five is to be steady and to
be realistic about what to expect.
I promise to be honest with you, so here
it is.
You will not eat peanut butter on Monday
and feel 20 years younger by Friday.
In the first couple of weeks, what many
people notice is simple. They feel full
between meals and they reach for fewer
sweet snacks. That makes sense because
of the protein, fat, and fiber, but it
is not something a big study proved. The
muscle study ran for 6 months. The big
studies on diabetes and heart disease
followed people for years, even decades.
This is a slow, steady habit, not a
quick fix.
If you want to see if your own numbers
change, ask your doctor to check your
cholesterol and blood sugar after a few
months of better eating.
And rule number six is to know your own
health. Peanut butter is not right for
everyone. If you have a peanut allergy,
please skip it. If you have kidney
disease, ask your doctor first because
peanut butter has potassium and
phosphorus, and some people need to
limit those.
If you take medicine for diabetes or you
eat a low-salt diet, check with your
doctor or a dietitian about how it fits.
And if you have trouble swallowing,
remember that thick peanut butter can
stick. Spread it thin or stir it into
oatmeal or yogurt, and talk to your
doctor. This video is general
information, not medical advice. Use it
as a starting point for a talk with the
people who know your health best. Look,
I could spend another hour on everything
in that jar and every study I read, but
here is what I really want you to take
away.
The biggest mistake older people make
with food is waiting.
Waiting for a diagnosis, waiting for a
symptom, waiting for someone to say
something is wrong before they start
doing something right.
Right now, your body is giving you a
window, a chance to build strength
before you need it. A chance to make
small, steady choices that can add up to
a very different life at 75 or 80.
Peanut butter is not magic, and it is
not the only thing you should do. But it
is one of the simplest, cheapest, most
studied foods you can buy, and it is
sitting on a shelf a few minutes from
your home for just a few dollars.
Check the label, pick the natural one,
swap it in for something less helpful,
and keep learning.
Now, I'd like to ask you for one small
favor. I put out a video like this every
week. I check the research carefully, I
explain it in plain words, and I leave
the warnings in because I believe you
deserve the truth.
If you got even one useful idea today,
please subscribe to this channel. It
costs you nothing, no fee, no sign up,
nothing to remember. But it means that
next week, when I share the next food,
habit, or study that could help you stay
strong and independent, it will be
waiting for you and not buried where
you'll never find it again.
And if you're thinking, "I'll do it
later," please do it right now, because
later is where good plans disappear.
Tap subscribe, tap the little bell, and
give this video a like. That helps it
reach other people who need it. And if
someone you love is over 60, send this
video to them. It might be the push they
need.
Your health is not one big choice. It is
thousands of small ones made every day
over many years.
The fact that you watched all the way to
the end tells me you are making good
ones. So, go check that label, make the
swap, and take care of yourself because
you are worth it. I'll see you in the
next video.

Can your sleeping position raise stroke risk after 60? In this video, I explain what the research really shows about sleeping positions, sleep apnea, snoring, and stroke risk overnight, and which common online claims are not proven.


Stroke risk overnight is a real concern, and many seniors search for the best sleeping position to protect themselves. But most online claims go further than the research does. In this video, I count down 5 sleep habits, and I label each one Proven, Plausible, or Unproven, so you know the difference between a warning and a guess. The one habit with strong evidence is sleep apnea, and back sleeping can make it worse if you snore.

IN THIS VIDEO
Why the early morning is a vulnerable window (the morning blood pressure surge)
Number 5: Sleeping with your arms above your head
Number 4: Sleeping on your stomach
Number 3: Cutting back on fluids in the evening
Number 2: Sleeping flat, and your morning blood pressure
Number 1: Back sleeping with snoring or sleep apnea, and the link between sleep apnea and stroke
Your plan for tonight, including the best sleeping position for seniors who snore
Left side or right side? What the research does and does not show
How to check your blood pressure at home
What to do if you wake up with stroke signs (FAST)
A 7-night plan, including when to ask your doctor about a sleep study for sleep apnea or a home sleep test



Tell me in the comments where you are watching from and how old you are, and subscribe so you don't miss the next video.



MEDICAL DISCLAIMER
This video is for education only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor about your sleep, your blood pressure, and your health.


SOURCES AND RESOURCES
Kario et al., Morning surge in blood pressure as a predictor of silent and clinical cerebrovascular disease in elderly hypertensives (Circulation, 2003)
Redline et al., Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea and incident stroke: the Sleep Heart Health Study (American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, 2010)
Yaggi et al., Obstructive sleep apnea as a risk factor for stroke and death (New England Journal of Medicine, 2005)
American Heart Association News, Can sleep position affect your heart and brain health? (January 2025)
American Heart Association scientific statement on sleep and brain health (2024)
Lee et al., The effect of body posture on brain glymphatic transport (Journal of Neuroscience, 2015; an animal study)
American Heart Association, Monitoring your blood pressure at home

#StrokePrevention #SleepApnea #SeniorHealth

are also, without knowing it, not
breathing. Not for a few seconds, for
10, 20, sometimes 40 seconds at a time.
Your oxygen drops, your brain sounds an
alarm, your heart rate and blood
pressure jump, then you gasp and fall
back asleep without remembering a thing.
Now picture that happening dozens of
times a night, always on your back.
Here is why it matters. Sleep apnea is a
proven risk factor for stroke and for
many people lying on the back makes it
much worse. But here's the part almost
nobody tells you. Most of what you read
online about sleeping positions and
stroke goes further than the research
does. Arms above your head, sleeping on
your stomach, sleeping flat. Some of
those claims are weak, some are simply
not proven. So today, I will sort it out
honestly. Five common sleep habits,
counted down from five to one and for
each one, I will tell you how strong the
evidence really is. One of them truly
deserves your attention and there is one
night time habit no pillow can fix. Stay
until the end.
Number one may be the most important
thing you hear this week. I'm Dr. Wade
Collins. On this channel, I explain
health to seniors in simple words so you
can protect your independence, your
strength and your quality of life.
Before we begin, tell me where you are
watching from and how old you are and
subscribe so you don't miss the next
video. I read every comment and reply to
each one. One honest line first, no
sleeping position can promise to prevent
a stroke. What a position can do is make
some health problems better or worse.
That is what we will look at. Let's
start with why night time matters for
your brain and your heart. Strokes and
heart attacks are more common in the
morning hours. A big part of that is
your body clock. Before you wake, your
blood pressure starts to climb and and
keeps climbing through the early
morning. That is normal. It is not
caused by getting out of bed, but in
some older adults, the climb is steep.
In a Japanese study of 519 older adults
with high blood pressure, average age
72, researchers followed them for about
3 and 1/2 years. The group with the
biggest morning surge had about 2.7
times the stroke risk of the others,
even after matching for age and 24-hour
blood pressure. That kind of study shows
a link. It does not prove the surge
alone causes strokes, but it tells us
the early morning is a vulnerable
window, and what happens overnight sets
it up. Here is how I will judge each
habit today. I will use three labels.
Proven means good human studies support
it. Plausible means it makes sense, but
it has not been proven in people.
Unproven means I could not find solid
evidence, because you deserve to know
the difference between a warning and a
guess. We start at number five. Number
five, sleeping with your arms above your
head.
You may have seen the claim, raised arms
squeeze the blood vessels under your
collarbone and strain your heart. It
sounds frightening, and it is
everywhere. I looked for evidence. I
could not find a study showing that
sleeping with raised arms raises the
risk of stroke or heart disease. So,
this one earns the label unproven.
Now, something real. Many people wake
with numb or tingling hands. That is
common, and it usually has simple
causes, such as pressure on a nerve at
the wrist, the elbow, or the neck. If it
happens often, mention it to your doctor
because treatments exist.
And one warning. Numbness or weakness
that comes on suddenly on one side of
the body, especially with a drooping
face or trouble speaking, is not a
sleeping problem. That is a stroke
warning, and you call your emergency
number.
If your raised arms bother your
shoulders, try hugging a pillow instead.
It is comfortable, and it costs nothing.
Next, a A many doctors quietly dislike.
Number four, sleeping on your stomach.
Imagine a woman named Joan. She is 67.
She is not a real patient, just an
example of what many people describe.
She has slept on her stomach all her
life, and lately she wakes with a stiff
neck and a dull headache.
Here is the claim you will hear.
Face down, your neck twists, and that
cuts the blood flow to your brain.
Is it true?
I could not find proof that stomach
sleeping raises stroke risk in people.
So, for stroke, the label is unproven.
There is one animal study worth knowing.
In anesthetized rats, scientists found
that the brain cleared waste more slowly
in the face-down position than on the
side. But, rats are not people, and the
researchers said it must be tested in
humans.
What is real is simpler. Stomach
sleeping keeps your neck turned for
hours, and for many people, that means
neck and back strain and morning
stiffness.
If that is you, side sleeping with a
pillow may feel better. Change slowly. A
habit of 60 years will not disappear in
one night. Start by hugging a pillow so
your body feels supported as you turn to
your side.
If you are still with me, type the
number four in the comments and
subscribe to the channel. I read every
comment and reply to each one.
Number three is something many seniors
do on purpose with good intentions, and
it may work against them.
Number three, cutting back on fluids in
the evening to avoid bathroom trips.
I understand why people do it. Nobody
wants to be up at 2:00 in the morning.
But, there is a trade-off.
When you are low on fluid, your blood
becomes slightly thicker, and your heart
works a bit harder. That makes sense on
paper, so the label is plausible. But, I
could not find a study showing that
limiting evening water causes stroke.
So, I won't tell you it does.
My advice is practical. Drink steadily
through the day so you are not catching
up at night. Many people also keep a
small glass of water by the bed to drink
on waking.
Now an important exception.
If your doctor has given you a fluid
limit because of heart failure or kidney
disease, follow it. Do not change it
because of a video, including this one.
And here is a clue worth knowing.
If you wake several times a night to
urinate, do not just blame age. It can
come from an enlarged prostate,
diabetes, heart failure, or sleep apnea.
Tell your doctor. It is a symptom worth
explaining, not just managing.
Next, a claim about your morning blood
pressure. Number two, sleeping flat and
what it does to your morning blood
pressure. The claim goes like this.
Lying flat plus blood pressure pills
causes the morning spike. So, you must
sleep propped up. Let's check it. The
morning surge is real. We talked about
it a few minutes ago, but it comes
largely from your body clock. It rises
with the dawn whether you lie flat or
propped up. I found no evidence that
sleeping flat causes the surge or that
raising your head prevents it. So, the
position claim is unproven. But the
surge itself is proven to matter. So,
what can you do?
You can measure it. Check your blood
pressure at home. Sit quietly for 5
minutes, feet flat, arms supported at
heart level, and no talking. Take two
readings, 1 minute apart, in the morning
before your medicines, and again in the
evening. Write them down for a week and
show your doctor.
And a clear rule. If your readings run
high in the morning, ask your doctor
whether the timing of your medicines
should change. Never change the timing
or the dose yourself.
One more exception. If you have acid
reflux or you feel short of breath when
you lie flat, raising the head of your
bed a little may feel better. That is a
comfort and symptom issue, so ask your
doctor what is right for you.
Quick question. Do you snore or has
anyone told you that you stop breathing
at night? Type snore or quiet in the
comments and subscribe to the channel. I
read every comment and reply to each
one.
Now, number one. The only item on this
list with strong evidence, and it is not
a position alone. It is a position plus
a hidden condition.
Number one, sleeping on your back when
you have loud snoring or sleep apnea.
Let me explain the condition first. In
obstructive sleep apnea, the soft tissue
at the back of your throat relaxes and
your airway narrows or closes.
Your breathing stops for 10, 20,
sometimes 40 seconds. Your oxygen dips,
your brain wakes you just enough to
breathe, and your body releases stress
hormones.
This can happen dozens of times a night
and most people never remember it.
Now, the evidence, and this part is
strong. In the Sleep Heart Health Study,
a large study supported by the US
National Heart, Lung, and Blood
Institute, men with moderate to severe
sleep apnea were nearly three times more
likely to have a stroke than men without
it. In women, the extra risk showed up
mainly with severe apnea. And in a study
from Yale, sleep apnea nearly doubled
the risk of stroke or death even after
the researchers adjusted for other risk
factors. So, sleep apnea earns the label
proven as a stroke risk factor.
And the position? A sleep researcher who
helped write an American Heart
Association statement says most people
with sleep apnea have much worse apnea
on their back than on their side. So,
the idea that back sleeping worsens
apnea is well supported.
Now, the honest limit. The same experts
say we do not yet know whether avoiding
back sleeping or any other apnea
treatment lowers the risk of stroke. So,
I cannot promise that moving to your
side prevents a stroke. What I can say
is that if you have sleep apnea, side
sleeping is a sensible step and it is
not harmful.
Here are the warning signs. loud snoring
gasping or choking at night or a partner
who sees you stop breathing. Waking up
with a headache or a dry mouth. Feeling
exhausted after a full night. Falling
asleep during the day. If that sounds
like you, call your doctor this week and
ask about a sleep test. Many can be done
at home. Treatment works, and the
standard treatment is CPAP, a mask that
keeps your airway open. For people whose
apnea happens mostly on their back,
doctors sometimes add position training.
And avoiding alcohol close to bedtime
helps because alcohol relaxes the
airway. This is the one item on the list
where a conversation with your doctor
can change your risk. So, what should
you actually do tonight? Here is the
plan, in order. First, if you snore or
you have sleep apnea, side sleeping is a
sensible default. Put a pillow between
your knees so your hips stay level. Hug
a body pillow in front of you so you
don't roll onto your stomach. Place a
pillow behind your back to make it
harder to roll flat. And keep your neck
straight with a pillow that fills the
space between your ear and your
shoulder. Second, if you don't snore and
you feel well, then the simplest advice
is also the best. Sleep in the position
that feels comfortable and lets you wake
up the least. That is the advice of the
sleep specialists I mentioned. Quality
sleep matters more than a perfect
position. Third, left side or right
side? You will hear strong opinions.
There is no good proof that one side
protects your heart or brain better.
Some people with reflux feel better on
the left. Some people with heart failure
feel more breathless on the left and
prefer the right. So, choose the side
that feels best. Fourth, the famous
brain cleaning claim. The study I
mentioned was done in rats. It found
that waste moved out of the brain most
efficiently when the animals lay on
their sides. It is interesting, but the
scientists said it needs to be tested in
people. So, please do not believe anyone
who tells you that sleeping on your side
prevents Alzheimer's. That has not been
shown.
Fifth, measure your mornings. Use the
home blood pressure routine I gave you
earlier and keep a short journal for a
week. Write down your bedtime, your wake
time, any morning headache, dizziness,
or tiredness, and your readings. Bring
it to your appointment. A doctor can do
a lot more with dates and numbers than
with I feel off.
Sixth, never stop or change a medicine
because of a sleep video. If you think
your medicine timing is a problem, ask
first. And one thing about quality, not
position. Go to bed and wake up at
regular times. Keep the room dark and
comfortable. Limit caffeine in the
afternoon. Good sleep habits help every
system in your body.
Now, one more thing, because this is
where seconds matter. If you ever wake
up with a stroke sign, remember the word
fast. Face drooping, arm weakness,
speech trouble. Time to call your
emergency number. Do not go back to
sleep and hope it passes. Do not wait
for it to get better. Do not drive
yourself. Call. And tell the emergency
team the last time you were known to be
completely well. If you woke up with
symptoms, that time is when you went to
bed. Stroke teams use it to decide which
treatments are possible, and some of
them only work within a limited window.
And if a stroke sign comes and then goes
within minutes, still call. That can be
a mini stroke, and it is a warning that
a bigger one may be coming.
Let me make this simple.
Pick one thing and try it for seven
nights.
If you snore, ask your partner to listen
for pauses or record a few minutes on
your phone and then call your doctor
about a sleep test.
If you wake with a stiff neck, try the
side position with a pillow between your
knees.
If your mornings feel off, keep a week
